content: Keratoconus is a progressive condition characterized by thinning and weakening of the cornea, the transparent front surface of the eye. Approximately 10% to 15% of individuals diagnosed with keratoconus eventually require corneal transplantation. This can involve either full-thickness transplantation, known as penetrating keratoplasty, or partial-thickness transplantation, referred to as deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK). The purpose of this study was to compare the visual outcomes of DALK and penetrating keratoplasty in patients with keratoconus. Additionally, the study aimed to evaluate other factors that may influence visual outcomes, such as astigmatism, graft rejection, and graft failure. A comprehensive search of electronic databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, and EMBASE, was conducted without restrictions on date or language. The last search was performed on October 31, 2013. Proceedings from international ophthalmic conferences were also manually reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing DALK and penetrating keratoplasty for keratoconus were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. For binary outcomes, such as graft failure, rejection, and achievement of functional vision, results were expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For continuous outcomes, such as postoperative best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA), keratometric astigmatism, and spherical equivalent, results were expressed as mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs. Two studies conducted in Iran met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 111 participants (30 in one study and 81 in the other). All participants had moderate to severe keratoconus and were randomly assigned to undergo either DALK or penetrating keratoplasty. Only one eye per participant was treated. The smaller study provided 12-month follow-up data for all participants, while the larger study reported follow-up durations ranging from 6.8 to 36.4 months, with all participants followed for at least three months after suture removal. In the larger study, four DALK procedures were abandoned due to technical difficulties, and visual and refractive outcomes were not measured for these cases. The smaller study did not provide details on the randomization process, so sensitivity analyses were performed to assess whether its inclusion influenced the overall results. Neither study found significant differences between the two surgical techniques in terms of post-graft visual outcomes, keratometric astigmatism, or spherical equivalent. One case of graft failure was reported in the penetrating keratoplasty group, while no graft failures occurred in the DALK groups of either study. Graft rejection was observed in both groups across both studies, but most cases were successfully managed with steroid treatment. The data indicated that rejection was less likely to occur following DALK compared to penetrating keratoplasty (OR: 0.33, 95% CI: 0.14 to 0.81, GRADE rating: moderate). Sensitivity analyses showed that the inclusion of data from one study (Razmju 2011) did not bias the results regarding rejection episodes. However, when analyzing graft failure rates, the data from the other study (Javadi 2010) alone had a wide 95% CI, indicating imprecision. Therefore, even after excluding the Razmju 2011 data, it remained challenging to draw definitive conclusions about the superiority of one technique over the other in terms of graft failure. DALK could not be completed as planned in four cases, and three additional cases required further intervention due to complications during the dissection process. Adverse events of varying severity were reported in both surgical groups with similar frequency. These included postoperative astigmatism, steroid-induced ocular hypertension, and persistent epithelial defects. In the DALK group, one participant developed interface neovascularization (growth of blood vessels at the junction of the host and donor cornea), and another experienced wrinkling of Descemet's membrane (the basement membrane separating the corneal stroma from the endothelium). In the penetrating keratoplasty group, one participant required graft resuturing, and another developed an atonic pupil (a dilated, non-reactive pupil). The overall quality of the evidence was rated as very low to moderate due to methodological limitations, incomplete data analysis, imprecision, and a high risk of bias in several areas across both studies. In conclusion, there was no evidence to suggest a difference in BCVA outcomes at three months post-graft or at any other analyzed time points (GRADE rating: very low). Similarly, no differences were found in graft survival, final UCVA, or keratometric outcomes. However, there was moderate-quality evidence suggesting that graft rejection is less likely to occur following DALK compared to penetrating keratoplasty. The limited number of studies and their methodological shortcomings mean that the overall quality of evidence is low. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to determine which surgical technique offers better overall outcomes for patients with keratoconus, including final visual acuity, time to achieve visual stability, keratometric stabilization, risk of rejection or failure, and risk of other adverse events. Large, well-designed randomized trials are needed to compare the outcomes of penetrating keratoplasty and DALK in the treatment of keratoconus.
